results.name: Inside Coruna and DarkSword Chains: From Web Lures to iOS Exploitation
results.description: Seven months after initial disclosure, the Coruna iOS exploit framework continues to evolve, now deploying two distinct chains based on device operating system version. Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework, while later builds receive DarkSword-derived chains. Analysis identified 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code, with 93 sites mapping to 21 distinct tracking collectors. Distribution spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and compromised legitimate sites. The attack requires no user interaction beyond loading a webpage, operating through hidden iframes that deploy browser exploits leading to native code execution. Recovered modules include kernel memory manipulation, code-signing enforcement changes, process memory access, encrypted command-and-control communication, and cleanup routines. results.name: Kairos Hold'em: Dissecting a New Go-Based DDoS Botnet
results.description: Kairos is a newly documented DDoS botnet for Linux written in Go, designed to transform compromised machines into attack nodes. The bot establishes hundreds to thousands of TCP connections to operator-specified targets, maintaining them with minimal keepalive bytes every few seconds to exhaust victim services. Initial access occurs via Telnet using default root credentials with empty passwords. The payload is delivered through multi-fallback shell commands via HTTP from the same server used for command and control. The bot operates with a simple three-command protocol including hold, kill all, and kill unpause commands. It masquerades as a kernel worker thread and employs a build-per-C2 distribution model, with samples identified across multiple CPU architectures including x86_64, ARM, MIPS, and 386.

results.name: Trojanized Claude Code Extension Plants an SSH Backdoor
results.description: Version 2.1.313 of the Claude Code extension in the Cursor Marketplace was compromised on October 29th, 2026. A malicious 66-line loader was inserted before legitimate extension code in the extension.js file. Upon activation, it adds an attacker-controlled SSH key labeled 'svc-telemetry' to the victim's authorized_keys, attempts to enable local SSH services, and establishes a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82.225. The implant collects reconnaissance data including hostname, user information, Git configuration, and environment variables containing credentials. It installs platform-specific persistence mechanisms using LaunchAgents on macOS, crontab on Linux, and scheduled tasks on Windows. Beacon data is transmitted unencrypted to the command-and-control infrastructure, providing persistent remote access through the established SSH tunnel.

results.name: Polymarket Breach Alert: Wallet-Draining Code Found in a Third-Party Script
results.description: A malicious JavaScript file was discovered in a third-party performance monitoring integration on Polymarket. The script, hosted on a DebugBear CDN URL, contained sophisticated code designed to access authenticated trading sessions, inspect user portfolios, and transfer cryptocurrency assets to attacker-controlled addresses. The payload searches for active trading clients and signers within the user's browser session, then attempts to sell positions or transfer tokens directly. Analysis revealed code that reads authentication context from local storage, traverses React component structures to locate trading functionality, and constructs EIP-712 signed messages to move assets. A fallback recipient address embedded in the script showed holdings exceeding $2.1 million. Production build metadata from Polymarket confirms removal of the DebugBear integration. While the script's malicious capabilities are established through static analysis, the total number of victims and aggregate losses remain unverified.

results.name: How Attackers Redirect Crypto Payments
results.description: Cryptocurrency transactions face unique threats from specialized malware known as Clipbankers, designed to redirect payments by replacing copied wallet addresses with attacker-controlled ones. These attacks exploit user trust in clipboard functions, the difficulty of memorizing long cryptographic strings, and the irreversible nature of blockchain transactions. Two prominent families, AnimateClipper and Efimer, demonstrate sophisticated capabilities including pattern matching and digit-matching techniques to minimize detection. AnimateClipper emerged in January 2026 and monitors clipboards for cryptocurrency patterns across multiple networks. Efimer employs advanced evasion techniques including Pyarmor protection, XOR encryption, and TOR-based command and control communications, while matching leading or trailing digits of addresses. results.name: Prediction Markets Emerge as a New Vertical for Traffer Teams
results.description: Multiple Russian-language traffer teams have rapidly adapted affiliate-fraud models to exploit growing interest in prediction markets like PolyMarket and Kalshi since spring 2026. Three teams—AtlasCore, PolyFucked, and Magnetic Team—provide comprehensive fraud infrastructure including websites, administrative panels, cryptocurrency payment systems, and technical support. These services enable affiliates to deploy convincing prediction-market interfaces combined with established fraud mechanisms such as controlled trading outcomes, fabricated market activity, artificial withdrawal restrictions, and collection of sensitive identity information. Artificial intelligence accelerates these operations by reducing time and expertise required for platform development, content creation, social engineering, and victim engagement. results.name: Aurora ransomware targets ESXi abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation
results.description: Aurora ransomware group has been active since approximately April 2026, targeting organizations across multiple countries and operating a data leak site. The investigation revealed the group deploys a Linux ransomware variant specifically designed for ESXi environments, using ChaCha20 encryption with RSA-4096 key wrapping. A distinctive characteristic includes the abuse of Cursor Agent with Claude Sonnet AI to assist with hands-on exploitation activities across ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The AI agent performed tasks including privilege enumeration, network scanning, NTLM relay attacks, and certificate attacks. Operators imposed specific restrictions prohibiting DCSync, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains. A second cluster of activity attributed to Aurora used different tactics including SQL Server lateral movement, GodPotato escalation, and S3-based exfiltration affecting eight organizations across multiple countries.

results.name: SEO Poisoning Campaign Targets DeepSeek Users: Chinese Threat Actor Deploys Kong RAT via Multi-Stage Attacks
results.description: A sophisticated SEO poisoning campaign targets users searching for DeepSeek AI tools through malicious lookalike domains positioned on first-page search results. The attack employs a multi-stage infection chain beginning with weaponized MSI files disguised as legitimate DeepSeek software. The execution flow progresses through multiple stages involving shellcode, DLL side-loading via legitimate Cyglaunch software, and ultimately deploys Kong RAT. The threat actor registered domains mimicking DeepSeek and distributed ZIP archives containing code-signed fake installers to add legitimacy. Attribution points to a potential Chinese threat actor based on PDB paths referencing '52pojie', a Chinese cybersecurity forum. This campaign appears to be a continuation of previous operations from April 2026 targeting users of Chinese developer tools including FinalShell SSH client, Xshell, and Clash proxy. The final payload includes keylogger functionality and establishes persistence through registry modifications.

results.name: Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497): Brotli RCE Exploited
results.description: A critical out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google's Brotli decompression library allows specially crafted compressed data to corrupt application memory, potentially enabling remote code execution. The flaw, scoring 9.2 CVSS v4.0, affects Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 and impacts multiple platforms including Node.js, Bun, Python implementations, and .NET frameworks. Exploitation attempts were observed within days of patch availability, with working proof-of-concept code demonstrating remote code execution against Node.js environments through malicious HTTP requests and responses. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on October 27, 2026. The vulnerability can be triggered through various attack vectors including incoming HTTP requests with Brotli-compressed bodies, malicious server responses, and file processing workflows. Enterprise products from Palo Alto Networks and VMware are also affected, expanding the attack surface beyond typical Node.js deployments.
